candidates.title: The Exploration Company to Test Lunar Hopper Demonstrator in 2027
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: The Exploration Company The Exploration Company has announced it will test a lunar hopper demonstrator called ONEIROS in the United Arab Emirates in 2027. ONEIROS is a privately funded initiative focused on validating technologies that could eventually support lower-cost access to the lunar surface. The company plans to build a one-tonne demonstrator that will use a throttleable methane-fuelled rocket engine, autonomous navigation, and hazard-avoidance systems to demonstrate the capabilities needed for controlled landings on the Moon. According to the abstract of a paper presented at the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Türkiye, work on the project began earlier this year. Teams have already built several breadboards to reduce technical risks ahead of the planned flight demonstration next year. The decision to conduct the flight demonstration in the UAE follows a memorandum of understanding signed with the country’s national space agency to support the project and develop local testing capabilities. While no subsequent binding agreement has been announced, the abstract confirmed that testing would take place in “the UAE desert.” The Exploration Company intends to follow ONEIROS with Hilal, a demonstrator designed to validate precision landing capabilities and methane/oxygen propulsion technologies on the Moon’s surface. The company will then move ahead with its full-scale Nyx Moon lander. Beyond its lunar lander programmes, The Exploration Company is also part of a consortium selected by the European Space Agency in February 2026 to conduct a Lunar Remote Camp study . Led by the Danish firm SAGA Space Architects, the consortium is developing a concept for a deployable lunar shelter that would initially support robotic operations, with the potential to accommodate astronauts during short stays on the lunar surface. candidates.title: DOT Proposes Changes to Part 450 Licensing Rules
candidates.raw_excerpt: The Department of Transportation is Marie Kondo-ing Part 450, keeping only what sparks safety. On Tuesday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced five proposed FAA rules aiming to streamline and modernize commercial space launch and reentry regulations. The rules are the first output from the aptly named USDOT Space Policy Administration, Coordination, and Execution—aka SPACE—Task Force. The proposals take aim at the Part 450 commercial space-licensing process, trying to balance efficiency and flexibility with existing safety standards. Updating the regs is intended to help industry meet the White House’s goal of 1,000 commercial launches and reentries per year by 2030. Task force: Launched on Sept. 9, the SPACE Task Force is an intradepartmental body that coordinates space policy on behalf of DOT. Its to-do list includes implementing the White House’s National Space Transportation Policy and leading a commercial space transportation strategy. The newly proposed changes to Part 450 include: Consolidating the documentation that operators submit for flight-safety analyses; Letting operators size flight-hazard areas by a vehicle’s maximum energy when they rely on physical containment, instead of a full probabilistic risk analysis; Exempting descending vehicles from extra lightning mitigation as long as they can’t leave an area from which the public was already cleared; Allowing operators to submit license applications electronically; Clarifying that far-field blast analyses must cover existing locations, not hypothetical ones. Redline: The proposals target how operators prove they meet FAA public-risk limits—and some update wording that was construed in a way the agency didn’t attend. For example, far-field blast analyses model the impact of a rocket explosion’s shock wave on windows miles away. candidates.title: Chinese scientists develop rice's full-lifecycle cell atlas
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Chinese researchers have developed the world's first three-dimensional spatiotemporal cell atlas that tracks the entire growth lifecycle of rice.

The landmark findings, published online Tuesday in the international journal Cell, resolve long-standing bottlenecks in observing and understanding how rice cells grow, divide and coordinate to shape the crop.

Led by Yazhouwan National Laboratory based in south China's Hainan Province, a consortium of 12 research institutions, including Chinese biotech firm BGI-Research and Huazhong Agricultural University, built a 3D spatiotemporal cell atlas covering rice's entire journey, from seed germination to flowering and grain filling. The resource supports future efforts to improve grain quality, according to the team.

Using the widely cultivated japonica rice variety Zhonghua 11 as the research subject, the scientists integrated self-developed spatial omics, single-cell omics and high-throughput sequencing technologies to build a comprehensive rice cell atlas.

Covering 10 types of rice organs and tissues and 61 continuous developmental stages, the atlas is built on more than 850,000 high-quality single-nucleus datasets and over 340,000 spatial data units. The team precisely identified and annotated 119 cell types and 133 cell subtypes, successfully matching each cell's molecular features with its spatial location and dynamic changes across growth stages.

candidates.title: NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission undocks from ISS for return to Earth
candidates.raw_excerpt:
NASA said its SpaceX Crew-12 mission undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Wednesday and began its journey back to Earth.

The SpaceX Dragon spacecraft carrying four astronauts undocked from the ISS at 8:05 a.m. Eastern Time (1205 GMT) to begin the journey home.

The spacecraft is scheduled to splash down off the coast of California at approximately 11:34 a.m. Thursday, marking the end of the Crew-12 mission's months-long stay in space, according to NASA.

The four-member crew consists of NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. The mission launched from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on February 13.

candidates.title: Azercosmos Launches AI Platform
candidates.raw_excerpt: Azercosmos has made a significant move in the AI arena. It has launched Platerra, an AI-powered platform designed to automatically analyze satellite imagery and turn it into geospatial information that can support decision-making across a range of applications. The company made the announcement, Oct. 7. Platerra combines Earth Observation (EO) data with AI to automate key stages of satellite imagery analysis. By reducing the need for fully manual interpretation, the platform aims to enable users to extract relevant information from imagery more quickly and efficiently. For Azercosmos, Platerra marks another step in combining space-based data with AI technologies. The platform is designed to expand the practical use of satellite imagery, improve access to processed geospatial information, and support faster decision-making. Azercosmos plans to continue developing Platerra by expanding its analytical capabilities and adding new applications in response to evolving user needs. The company sees growing international interest in geospatial AI, or GeoAI, as organizations seek more efficient ways to process increasing volumes of EO data. It believes AI-based analysis can help make satellite-derived information more accessible and easier to apply in both operational and strategic decision-making. candidates.title: Finland Orders Google to Suspend New Data Centers After Contractors Pave Over Protected Forests
candidates.raw_excerpt: Finish environmental authorities are in a rage over Google’s $15 billion data center projects after the discovery that company contractors had chopped down some 330 hectares of government-protected forests, seemingly without a permit. According to Agence France-Presse , the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) demanded that the Google-affiliate company Tuike Finland Oy “immediately suspend… all preparatory measures that would significantly alter the environment” in connection with two planned data center developments in the Northern municipalities of Muhos and Kajaani. In all, LVV accuses Google’s contractor of clear-cutting some 330 hectares in Muhos without completing a mandatory environmental impact assessment, a necessary step for receiving approval. The company cleared a further 200 hectares for its data center in Kajaani, though it isn’t clear whether that logging was approved by authorities. As the Guardian reported , Google has just over a week to explain its actions to Finnish officials. Though a government review is only just getting underway, the tech giant is already expressing remorse. In a statement to AFP , Google spokesperson Sondre Ronander admitted the company messed up, saying “we understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance.” “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance,” Ronander continued. As head of the environmental department of the LVV Tommi Muilu told AFP , Google has not only felled hundreds of acres of trees, but has stripped topsoil, engineered roads and storage areas, and altered ditches. Speaking to AFP , chair of the long-running Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said Google had paved over “nature sites which should be preserved.” More on data centers: Amazon Warns Local Communities to Stop Defying Its Massive AI Data Centers The post Finland Orders Google to Suspend New Data Centers After Contractors Pave Over Protected Forests appeared first on Futurism .

SpaceX filed for this constellation in September of last year , shortly after announcing the spectrum deal with EchoStar . With this action, SpaceX is authorized to deploy a constellation of 15,000 Non-Geostationary Orbit (NGSO) satellites to provide SCS and MSS within the U.S., MSS and direct-to-cell outside of the United States, and fixed satellite services (FSS) backhaul and telemetry, tracking, and command (TT&C). The satellites are all intended to operate in Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO), in nine orbital shells between 326 km to 335 km. The FCC stated in its Oct. 6 approval that this deployment will improve competition and give consumers more choices in more places, arguing the decision is in the public interest. “[This decision] will pave the way for SpaceX’s next-generation D2D network to extend spectrum based services to mobile systems. candidates.title: ChatGPT Caught Putting Signatures of Real Cartoonists on AI-Generated Comics
candidates.raw_excerpt: They say imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, but an AI model straight-up impersonating a humble cartoonist is probably not what that adage was going for. When a kitschy cartoon tribute to the recently deceased Dolly Parton and Tim Curry — dressed as Dr Frank-N-Furter from the 1975 cult classic “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” — going to heaven together went viral, New Yorker cartoonist Brendan Loper started getting messages from friends, family, and fans about whether he made it. After all, there was his unmistakable signature right there in the bottom corner: “BLOPER.” But he had nothing to do with the cartoon. Some grieving Parton fam had cooked it up in ChatGPT and posted it online, before it blew up. “It was very surreal,” he told Nieman Lab . ChatGPT, it turned out, has a predilection for crediting Loper for stuff he didn’t make. In May, someone warned him about another image created by the OpenAI chatbot that had his name on it. Actually, it really likes impersonating New Yorker cartoonists in general. There are also images with the signatures of the magazine’s longtime comic artists Harry Bliss, Emily Flake, Joe Dator, Pat Byrnes, Peter Vey, and Jason Adam Katzenstein, Nieman Lab found. Loper was well aware his work was “getting harvested for all of this [AI] training,” but felt his autograph being faked crossed a line. “I’m not a territorial person, but my name is my name. It felt very much like a violation of my personhood.” These signatures are maybe the most on the nose reminder of how AI models were trained on a vast corpus of writing, images, videos, and artworks that were scraped without permission.  The recreation of their signatures adds another thorny legal dimension on top of the potential copyright infringement involved. That choice of legal basis has consequences. The act’s architecture must be built around the provision of services. This creates a central question of scope. An operator operating its own satellite is not providing a service to a third party, unlike, e.g., an operator providing launch services. The proposal addresses that challenge by coupling the regulation of upstream activities with downstream provision of space-based data in the Union: space activities that generate space-based data provided in the EU market are subject to the EU Space Act as well. A paper published in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment on October 6, argues that ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) could help communities meet climate targets, provided projects demonstrate a net carbon benefit and acceptable environmental impacts.

The technique increases seawater's alkalinity, or its ability to neutralize acid, allowing it to absorb and store more CO2. It has drawn interest as a potential means of removing billions of tonnes of the gas from the atmosphere each year.

But turning that potential into practical projects requires a better understanding of local waters, ecosystems and available resources, the researchers say.

candidates.title: 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded for autocatalysis discovery
candidates.raw_excerpt:
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis."

Some molecules, including amino acids, exist as two variants that are each other's mirror image. However, living organisms only contain one of these mirror images. This chemical asymmetry, known as homochirality, has long puzzled scientists.

The Nobel Prize recognizes discoveries that have enabled chemists to steer chemical reactions toward producing one mirror-image form. This is particularly important in developing pharmaceuticals, where only one mirror image of a molecule may have the desired effect.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular," said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.

Their work has helped explain how chemical asymmetry can emerge and given chemists greater control over asymmetric reactions.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ArianeGroup / SSC Space The European Space Agency announced that ArianeGroup and SSC Space completed a second wet dress rehearsal of the Themis reusable rocket demonstrator at Esrange in Sweden. As with the first wet dress rehearsal , completed in July, the demonstrator was filled with liquid nitrogen rather than propellant. The nitrogen was cooled to around -200°C, allowing teams to test the vehicle and ground infrastructure under similar cryogenic temperatures and pressures without the added risk of propellant loading. The second rehearsal also included tests of elements of the automated ground systems developed to support reusable operations. After the demonstrator touches down following a test, robotic systems are expected to locate the vehicle, connect to it, and drain any remaining fuel and oxidiser while personnel remain at a safe distance. Previously, ESA said a hot-fire test of the demonstrator’s Prometheus engine would follow a full wet dress rehearsal using liquid oxygen and liquid methane. According to a statement from the SALTO consortium, “teams are now working on defining a window for the next test.” The consortium is conducting the initial Themis flight campaign under the European Union-funded SALTO initiative. The €42.8-million project is funding the first two low-altitude hop tests of Themis to demonstrate that the vehicle can be launched, recovered, and then launched again. During the first of those flights, Themis is expected to climb to an altitude of up to 100 metres before descending and attempting a vertical landing. The deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” per the Moscow Times — a vague diagnosis that left plenty of questions unanswered. The Black Death, a global 14th century pandemic that’s believed to have killed tens of millions of people, included all three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic. candidates.raw_excerpt: The “fair use” doctrine under the US Copyright Act of 1976 allows for copyrighted materials to be used for purposes like criticism, journalism, and research. Whether something is deemed fair use depends on several factors, including how transformative it is, how much of the work is used, and whether the reproduction alters the market value of the original. It’s the keystone of the AI industry’s legal defense in a litany of ongoing lawsuits filed by rightsholders, who are accusing tech companies of unlawfully using their intellectual property to train their AI models. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has long maintained that the AI race would be “over ” if this key provision of copyright law were ever overturned. After all, with legal precedent, AI companies like OpenAI could finally be held accountable for shamelessly crawling the entire web, including vast swathes of copyrighted materials, to shovel into the maws of their AI models. Now, the legal system is starting to show signs that the defense could be on thin ice. Last week, a US appeals court upheld a ruling that AI legal research company Ross Intelligence had broken copyright law by training its legal search engine on materials taken from Thomson Reuters’ Westlaw legal research platform and database. Ross shut down in 2021, shortly after the lawsuit was filed, citing mounting financial strains caused by the litigation. The decision by the Third Circuit court of appeals — a first-of-its-kid ruling, per Reuters — marks a pivotal, albeit heavily nuanced, moment in the ongoing fight between AI companies and rights holders, who accuse the former of unfairly taking advantage of their work.
